question: What is the main difference between structural heart disorders and electrical heart problems?

options.A: Structural disorders involve physical defects in heart valves, walls, or muscle.
options.B: Structural disorders can never be present at birth.
options.C: Electrical problems always require open-heart surgery.
options.D: Electrical problems only affect the right side of the heart.

explanation: Think of structural heart issues as physical problems with the heart's building blocks (like valves or walls), while electrical problems mess up the heart's natural wiring and rhythm. You've got this! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which of these is an example of a structural heart problem that develops later in life (acquired)?

options.A: Tetralogy of Fallot malformation
options.B: Degenerative calcific aortic valve stenosis
options.C: Ventricular septal defect present at birth
options.D: Atrial septal defect from fetal development

explanation: Acquired conditions happen over time due to aging or wear and tear, unlike congenital defects that babies are born with. Great job working through this! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h1)

question: When a heart valve is narrowed and blocked, what kind of extra strain does it put on the heart?

options.A: Electrical overload
options.B: Perfusion overload
options.C: Volume overload
options.D: Pressure overload

explanation: When a valve is narrowed, the heart has to push much harder to squeeze blood through it. That extra resistance creates a pressure overload! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h2)

question: If a patient has a leaky heart valve that lets blood flow backward, what main change happens to that heart chamber?

options.A: Instant muscle atrophy
options.B: Volume overload and chamber dilation
options.C: Complete electrical shutdown
options.D: Immediate valve healing

explanation: A leaky valve means extra blood flows backward into the chamber. This extra volume stretches and enlarges (dilates) the heart muscle over time. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h2)

question: What actually happens to a heart valve when a patient has stenosis?

options.A: It becomes stiff and fails to open fully.
options.B: It dissolves completely into the bloodstream.
options.C: It turns into muscle tissue.
options.D: It fails to close and leaks backward.

explanation: Stenosis simply means narrowing or stiffness. The valve flaps get stiff and won't swing wide open, making it hard for blood to flow forward. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h3)

question: What do we call a heart valve that doesn't seal tightly and lets blood slip backward?

options.A: Regurgitation
options.B: Hypertrophy
options.C: Stenosis
options.D: Atresia

explanation: Regurgitation (or a leaky valve) happens when the flaps don't close all the way, allowing blood to flow backward when it should be trapped. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h3)

question: An abnormal hole between the two lower chambers (ventricles) of the heart is known as:

options.A: Ventricular septal defect
options.B: Atrial septal defect
options.C: Aortic stenosis
options.D: Mitral regurgitation

explanation: A ventricular septal defect (VSD) is just an opening in the wall (septum) separating the right and left lower chambers. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why does a baby with Tetralogy of Fallot sometimes turn very blue when crying?

options.A: The lungs suddenly fill with large amounts of clear fluid.
options.B: Deoxygenated blood mixes and enters the systemic circulation.
options.C: The heart stops beating completely for several minutes.
options.D: Blood flow to the brain increases too quickly.

explanation: Because of the heart defects in Tetralogy of Fallot, oxygen-poor blood bypasses the lungs and goes straight out to the body, giving the skin a bluish tint. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which type of cardiomyopathy involves abnormal thickening of the heart muscle walls?

options.A: Ischemic cardiomyopathy
options.B: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
options.C: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
options.D: Dilated cardiomyopathy

explanation: 'Hyper-' means over or excessive, and 'trophic' relates to growth. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy means the heart muscle has grown too thick! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h5)

question: How does restrictive cardiomyopathy mainly affect the heart?

options.A: It thins out the walls until the heart bursts.
options.B: It makes the muscle rigid, preventing normal ventricular filling.
options.C: It causes the heart valves to dissolve rapidly.
options.D: It speeds up the electrical conduction pathways permanently.

explanation: In restrictive cardiomyopathy, the heart muscle becomes stiff and rigid. Because it can't relax, the chambers struggle to fill up with blood. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which sign is a classic clue of right-sided heart congestion?

options.A: Complete loss of vision in both eyes
options.B: Sudden wheezing and frothy pink sputum
options.C: Severe sharp chest pain radiating to the jaw
options.D: Peripheral edema and jugular venous distension

explanation: When the right side backs up, blood dams up in the body's veins. This leads to swollen ankles (edema) and bulging neck veins (jugular venous distension). [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h6)

question: Why do patients with heart valve problems often develop a heart murmur?

options.A: The electrical wires in the heart rub against each other.
options.B: Turbulent blood flow occurs as blood moves through narrowed or leaky valves.
options.C: Air gets trapped inside the heart muscle tissue.
options.D: The lungs make whistling sounds during deep breathing.

explanation: Normally, blood flows smoothly and quietly. But when it's forced through a tight or leaky valve, it splashes around and makes a WHOOSH sound—which we call a murmur! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main test used to diagnose structural heart valve problems?

options.A: Echocardiogram
options.B: Routine head CT scan
options.C: Standard skin biopsy
options.D: Abdominal ultrasound

explanation: An echo is an ultrasound of the heart! It lets doctors actually see the heart valves moving and check how well blood is flowing. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h7)

question: What extra information does a cardiac catheterization give you that a standard ECG doesn't?

options.A: Direct pressure measurements inside the heart chambers
options.B: The exact heart rate and rhythm over time
options.C: Surface signs of heart muscle inflammation
options.D: Electrical impulse timing across the atria

explanation: An ECG shows electrical activity on the skin, but a catheter goes right inside the heart to measure actual pressures and blood flow. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why do doctors give diuretics to patients with heart structural disorders?

options.A: To repair torn heart valve leaflets
options.B: To reduce fluid overload and congestion
options.C: To speed up the heart rate significantly
options.D: To cure congenital holes in the heart

explanation: Diuretics are 'water pills.' They help the kidneys flush out extra salt and water, clearing up swelling and fluid overload. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h8)

question: Why are beta-blockers commonly prescribed for structural heart conditions?

options.A: To dilate peripheral arteries and eliminate all body fat
options.B: To slow the heart rate and allow better ventricular filling time
options.C: To stimulate faster electrical firing from the sinus node
options.D: To thin the blood and stop all clot formation instantly

explanation: Slowing the heart down gives the ventricles more time to relax and fill up with blood, while also giving the tired heart muscle a bit of a break. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h8)

question: What are the two main types of artificial replacement valves used in heart surgery?

options.A: Mechanical and bioprosthetic
options.B: Autologous skin and muscle
options.C: Silicone and nylon mesh
options.D: Plastic and synthetic rubber

explanation: Replacement valves are either mechanical (made of tough man-made materials) or bioprosthetic (crafted from animal tissue, like pig or cow tissue). [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h9)

question: Which of these conditions is most likely to need a surgical valve repair or replacement?

options.A: Simple ventricular ectopic beats
options.B: Severe aortic stenosis
options.C: Controlled essential hypertension
options.D: Mild sinus tachycardia

explanation: When a valve is severely narrowed (stenosis), blood can't get through properly. Surgery is often needed to fix or replace that physical blockage. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h9)

question: What is an important long-term instruction for a patient who just received a mechanical heart valve?

options.A: Never drinking pure water again
options.B: Avoiding all forms of physical movement forever
options.C: Stopping daily blood pressure checks at home
options.D: The need for lifelong anticoagulation therapy

explanation: Blood loves to stick to artificial surfaces! Patients with mechanical valves must take blood thinners (anticoagulants) for the rest of their lives to prevent dangerous clots. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h10)

question: Why must patients with repaired heart defects take antibiotics before certain dental procedures?

options.A: To prevent infective endocarditis from bacteria entering the bloodstream
options.B: To lower their systemic blood pressure during the dental work
options.C: To keep their surgical chest incision from becoming dry
options.D: To prevent future heart rhythm changes after dental cleaning

explanation: Dental work can release bacteria into the blood. If it lands on repaired heart tissue, it can cause a serious infection called endocarditis. A dose of antibiotics keeps them safe! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T5#GNS213_U1_T5_h10)
